title: Reheating after Inflation
abstract:
The theory of reheating of the Universe after inflation is developed. The
transition from inflation to the hot Universe turns out to be strongly
model-dependent and typically consists of several stages. Immediately after
inflation the field $\phi$ begins rapidly rolling towards the minimum of its
effective potential. Contrary to some earlier expectations, particle production
during this stage does not lead to the appearance of an extra friction term
$\Gamma\dot\phi$ in the equation of motion of the field $\phi$. Reheating
becomes efficient only at the next stage, when the field $\phi$ rapidly
oscillates near the minimum of its effective potential. We have found that
typically in the beginning of this stage the classical inflaton field $\phi$
very rapidly (explosively) decays into $\phi$-particles or into other bosons
due to broad parametric resonance. This stage cannot be described by the
standard elementary approach to reheating based on perturbation theory. The
bosons produced at this stage, as well as some part of the classical field
$\phi$ which survives the stage of explosive reheating, should further decay
into other particles, which eventually become thermalized. The last stages of
decay can be described in terms of perturbation theory. Complete reheating is
possible only in those theories where a single massive $\phi$-particle can
decay into other particles. This imposes strong constraints on the structure of
inflationary models. On the other hand, this means that a scalar field can be a
cold dark matter candidate even if it is strongly coupled to other fields.
summary:
"Physicists propose new theory on Universe's reheating after inflation

A team led by scientists Lev Kofman, Andrei Linde, and Alexei A. Starobinsky challenges the conventional understanding of how the Universe transitioned from an inflating state to a hot one. The study introduces a series of stages in this reheating process.

Unlike previous assumptions, the researchers found that particle production during the initial stage does not introduce an additional friction term into the equation of motion for the field $\phi$. Efficient reheating occurs only at a subsequent phase, when $\phi$ rapidly oscillates near its effective potential's minimum. This rapid decay of classical inflaton field $\phi$ is said to result in a 'explosive' production of $\phi$-particles or other bosons due to broad parametric resonance."

title: <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>CPT</mml:mi></mml:math>violation and the standard model
abstract:
Spontaneous CPT breaking arising in string theory has been suggested as a
possible observable experimental signature in neutral-meson systems. We provide
a theoretical framework for the treatment of low-energy effects of spontaneous
CPT violation and the attendant partial Lorentz breaking. The analysis is
within the context of conventional relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum
field theory in four dimensions. We use the framework to develop a
CPT-violating extension to the minimal standard model that could serve as a
basis for establishing quantitative CPT bounds.

This work could pave the way for establishing new bounds on CPT symmetry, a critical principle in physics that ensures the conservation of energy, momentum, and charge during any physical transformation. The researchers propose a CPT-violating extension to the standard model, offering a potential basis for future experimental testing of these intriguing ideas.

title: The ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC
abstract: ALICE (A Large Ion Collider Experiment) is a general-purpose, heavy-ion detector at the CERN LHC which focuses on QCD, the strong-interaction sector of the Standard Model. It is designed to address the physics of strongly interacting matter and the quark-gluon plasma at extreme values of energy density and temperature in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Besides running with Pb ions, the physics programme includes collisions with lighter ions, lower energy running and dedicated proton-nucleus runs. ALICE will also take data with proton beams at the top LHC energy to collect reference data for the heavy-ion programme and to address several QCD topics for which ALICE is complementary to the other LHC detectors. The ALICE detector has been built by a collaboration including currently over 1000 physicists and engineers from 105 Institutes in 30 countries. Its overall dimensions are 16 × 16 × 26 m3 with a total weight of approximately 10 000 t. The experiment consists of 18 different detector systems each with its own specific technology choice and design constraints, driven both by the physics requirements and the experimental conditions expected at LHC. The most stringent design constraint is to cope with the extreme particle multiplicity anticipated in central Pb-Pb collisions. The different subsystems were optimized to provide high-momentum resolution as well as excellent Particle Identification (PID) over a broad range in momentum, up to the highest multiplicities predicted for LHC. This will allow for comprehensive studies of hadrons, electrons, muons, and photons produced in the collision of heavy nuclei. Most detector systems are scheduled to be installed and ready for data taking by mid-2008 when the LHC is scheduled to start operation, with the exception of parts of the Photon Spectrometer (PHOS), Transition Radiation Detector (TRD) and Electro Magnetic Calorimeter (EMCal). These detectors will be completed for the high-luminosity ion run expected in 2010. This paper describes in detail the detector components as installed for the first data taking in the summer of 2008.
summary:
Paper Title: New Detector at LHC to Probe Quark-Gluon Plasma

In a joint effort by over 1,000 scientists and engineers from 30 countries, a new experiment called ALICE has been established at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) by the CERN team. The experiment, focusing on Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), aims to study the physics of strongly interacting matter and the quark-gluon plasma at unprecedented energy levels.

ALICE is a general-purpose detector designed for heavy-ion collisions utilizing Pb ions, as well as lighter ions, lower energy running, and dedicated proton-nucleus runs. The detector will also collect data with high-energy proton beams to provide reference data and investigate several QCD topics that are complementary to the other LHC detectors.

Boasting a dimension of 16m x 16m x 26m and an approximate weight of 10,000 tons, ALICE consists of 18 different detector systems each designed to provide high-momentum resolution and excellent Particle Identification over a broad momentum range. These state-of-the-art subsystems will allow comprehensive studies of hadrons, electrons, muons, and photons produced in heavy nuclei collisions.

While most detector systems are scheduled for installation by mid-2008 when the LHC is expected to begin operation, some parts of the Photon Spectrometer (PHOS), Transition Radiation Detector (TRD), and Electro Magnetic Calorimeter (EMCal) will be completed later in 2010 for high-luminosity ion runs. The detailed description of this new detector component installation is outlined in a recent paper published in the Journal of Instrumentation.

title: FIVE-YEARWILKINSON MICROWAVE ANISOTROPY PROBEOBSERVATIONS: LIKELIHOODS AND PARAMETERS FROM THEWMAPDATA
abstract: This paper focuses on cosmological constraints derived from analysis of WMAP data alone. A simple LCDM cosmological model fits the five-year WMAP temperature and polarization data. The basic parameters of the model are consistent with the three-year data and now better constrained: Omega_b h^2 = 0.02273+-0.00062, Omega_c h^2 = 0.1099+-0.0062, Omega_L = 0.742+-0.030, n_s = 0.963+0.014- 0.015, tau = 0.087+-0.017, sigma_8 = 0.796+-0.036. With five years of polarization data, we have measured the optical depth to reionization, tau>0, at 5 sigma significance. The redshift of an instantaneous reionization is constrained to be z_reion = 11.0+-1.4 with 68% confidence. This excludes a sudden reionization of the universe at z=6 at more than 3.5 sigma significance, suggesting that reionization was an extended process. Using two methods for polarized foreground cleaning we get consistent estimates for the optical depth, indicating an error due to foreground treatment of tau~0.01. This cosmological model also fits small-scale CMB data, and a range of astronomical data measuring the expansion rate and clustering of matter in the universe. We find evidence for the first time in the CMB power spectrum for a non-zero cosmic neutrino background, or a background of relativistic species, with the standard three light neutrino species preferred over the best-fit LCDM model with N_eff=0 at >99.5% confidence, and N_eff > 2.3 (95% CL) when varied. The five-year WMAP data improve the upper limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio to r < 0.43 (95% CL), for power-law models. With longer integration we find no evidence for a running spectral index, with dn_s/dlnk = -0.037+-0.028.
summary:
Headline: "New Analysis of WMAP Data Sheds Light on Cosmic Reionization and Neutrino Background"

Summary: In a groundbreaking study published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, researchers led by J. Dunkley have found significant improvements in the analysis of data from the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP). By focusing on cosmological constraints derived from five years of WMAP temperature and polarization data, they have updated basic parameters of a simple LCDM cosmological model, including the reionization optical depth which is now measured at a 5 sigma significance. The redshift of an instantaneous reionization has been constrained to be z_reion = 11.0+-1.4, challenging the theory that the universe's reionization was sudden and suggesting instead that it may have been an extended process. Additionally, the study provides compelling evidence for a non-zero cosmic neutrino background, or a background of relativistic species, with more light neutrinos preferred over the standard three light neutrinos (N_eff>2.3 at 95% confidence). The improved data has also allowed researchers to tighten the upper limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio to r < 0.43 for power-law models.

title: The Interacting Boson Model
abstract: The interacting boson model was introduced in 1974 as an attempt to describe collective properties of nuclei in a unified way. Since 1974, the model has been the subject of many investigations and it has been extended to cover most aspects of nuclear structure. This book gives an account of the properties of the interacting boson model. In particular, this book presents the mathematical techniques used to analyze the structure of the model. It also collects in a single, easily accessible reference all the formulas that have been developed throughout the years to account for collective properties of nuclei. Suitable for both theorists and experimentalists.

The book provides an in-depth look at the mathematical techniques utilized to understand the model's structure, as well as a compilation of formulas developed over the years to account for collective properties of nuclei. title: Relativistic hadron-hadron collisions in the ultra-relativistic quantum molecular dynamics model
abstract: Hadron-hadron collisions at high energies are investigated in the Ultrarelativistic-Quantum-Molecular-Dynamics approach. This microscopic transport model describes the phenomenology of hadronic interactions at low and intermediate energies ( √ s &lt; 5 GeV) in terms of interactions between known hadrons and their resonances. At higher energies, √ s&gt; 5 GeV, the excitation of color strings and their subsequent fragmentation into hadrons dominates the multiple production of particles in the UrQMD model. The model shows a fair overall agreement with a large body of experimental h-h data over a wide range of h-h center-of-mass energies. Hadronic reaction data with higher precision would be useful to support the use of the UrQMD model for relativistic heavy ion collisions. PACS: 24.10.Lx, 13.75.-n, 13.85.-t 2 I.
summary:
Researchers led by Marcus Bleicher propose a new approach to studying high-energy hadron-hadron collisions using the Ultrarelativistic Quantum Molecular Dynamics (UrQMD) model, published in Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics.

The study builds on prior work in hadronic interactions at lower energies, where known hadrons and their resonances interact. At higher energies above 5 GeV, color strings are excites and fragmented into various hadrons in the UrQMD model, aiding in understanding multiple particle production.

While showing a general agreement with experimental data, the authors suggest improved precision in hadronic reaction data could further support the application of the UrQMD model for analyzing relativistic heavy ion collisions.

title: Single Silver Nanoparticles as Real-Time Optical Sensors with Zeptomole Sensitivity
abstract: This work utilizes dark-field optical microscopy to demonstrate the localized surface plasmon resonance ìmax response of individual Ag nanoparticles to the formation of a monolayer of small-molecule adsorbates. The adsorption of fewer than 60 000 1-hexadecanethiol molecules on single Ag nanoparticles results in a localized surface plasmon resonance shift of 40.7 nm. Additionally, the kinetics of the single nanoparticle response was shown to be comparable to that of other real-time sensor technologies. Noble-metal nanoparticles have extraordinary size-dependent optical properties that have been the subject of extensive studies.1-4 Specifically, these nanoparticles exhibit a strong UV-visible extinction band that is not present in the spectrum of the bulk metal. This extinction band results when the incident photon frequency is resonant with the collective excitation of the conduction electrons and is known as the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR). LSPR excita-tion results in wavelength-selective absorption with extremely large molar extinction coefficients (3 1011 M-1 cm-1),5
summary:
**Scientists Develop Nanoparticle Sensors with Unprecedented Sensitivity**

In a groundbreaking study published in the journal *Nano Letters*, researchers from Duke University led by Adam D. McFarland and Richard P. Van Duyne have created real-time optical sensors using single silver nanoparticles sensitive to zeptomole quantities (a trillionth of a mole).

The study, titled "Single Silver Nanoparticles as Real-Time Optical Sensors with Zeptomole Sensitivity," builds upon prior work on the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) in noble metal nanoparticles. Leveraging dark-field optical microscopy, the scientists demonstrated how a shift in LSPR occurs when a monolayer of small molecules adsorbs onto individual Ag nanoparticles.

With a mere 60,000 1-hexadecanethiol molecules causing a 40.7 nm resonance shift, the new sensor's kinetics are on par with other real-time sensing technologies. These findings represent a quantum leap in materials science and sensor technology as they offer exceptional sensitivity, paving the way for potential applications in various fields such as biomedicine, environmental monitoring, and security.

title: A theory of dark matter
abstract: We propose a comprehensive theory of dark matter that explains the recent proliferation of unexpected observations in high-energy astrophysics. Cosmic ray spectra from ATIC and PAMELA require a WIMP with mass M_chi ~ 500 - 800 GeV that annihilates into leptons at a level well above that expected from a thermal relic. Signals from WMAP and EGRET reinforce this interpretation. Taken together, we argue these facts imply the presence of a GeV-scale new force in the dark sector. The long range allows a Sommerfeld enhancement to boost the annihilation cross section as required, without altering the weak scale annihilation cross section during dark matter freezeout in the early universe. If the dark matter annihilates into the new force carrier, phi, its low mass can force it to decay dominantly into leptons. If the force carrier is a non-Abelian gauge boson, the dark matter is part of a multiplet of states, and splittings between these states are naturally generated with size alpha m_phi ~ MeV, leading to the eXciting dark matter (XDM) scenario previously proposed to explain the positron annihilation in the galactic center observed by the INTEGRAL satellite. Somewhat smaller splittings would also be expected, providing a natural source for the parameters of the inelastic dark matter (iDM) explanation for the DAMA annual modulation signal. Since the Sommerfeld enhancement is most significant at low velocities, early dark matter halos at redshift ~10 potentially produce observable effects on the ionization history of the universe, and substructure is more detectable than with a conventional WIMP. Moreover, the low velocity dispersion of dwarf galaxies and Milky Way subhalos can greatly increase the substructure annihilation signal.
summary:
Headline: New Theory of Dark Matter Proposed to Explain Astrophysical Observations

Summary:
In a groundbreaking paper published in Physical Review D, physicists Nima Arkani-Hamed, Douglas P. Finkbeiner, Tracy R. Slatyer, and Neal Weiner propose a novel theory of dark matter that could explain a series of unexpected high-energy astrophysical observations. The researchers suggest the presence of a GeV-scale new force in the dark sector, a WIMP with mass between 500 and 800 GeV annihilating into leptons at levels above thermal relic expectations. This theory could provide support for the eXciting dark matter (XDM) scenario and inelastic dark matter (iDM) explanations for various astrophysical phenomena, such as the positron annihilation in the galactic center and the DAMA annual modulation signal. The proposed theory also suggests that early dark matter halos at redshift ~10 could produce observable effects on the ionization history of the universe, while increasing substructure detectability in dwarf galaxies and Milky Way subhalos.

title: First Results from the LUX Dark Matter Experiment at the Sanford Underground Research Facility
abstract: The Large Underground Xenon (LUX) experiment is a dual-phase xenon time-projection chamber operating at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Lead, South Dakota). The LUX cryostat was filled for the first time in the underground laboratory in February 2013. We report results of the first WIMP search data set, taken during the period from April to August 2013, presenting the analysis of 85.3 live days of data with a fiducial volume of 118 kg. A profile-likelihood analysis technique shows our data to be consistent with the background-only hypothesis, allowing 90% confidence limits to be set on spin-independent WIMP-nucleon elastic scattering with a minimum upper limit on the cross section of 7.6 × 10(-46) cm(2) at a WIMP mass of 33 GeV/c(2). We find that the LUX data are in disagreement with low-mass WIMP signal interpretations of the results from several recent direct detection experiments.
summary:
Scientists Report First Results from Dark Matter Experiment, LUX

In an important breakthrough for physics, a global team of researchers have published their first findings from the Large Underground Xenon (LUX) experiment at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. The groundbreaking work, detailed in Physical Review Letters, seeks to unravel the mystery of dark matter, using advanced nuclear technology and a cryostat.

During the six-month period from April to August 2013, the researchers captured data equivalent to 85.3 live days with a focus volume of approximately 118 kg. Their analysis, employing a sophisticated profile-likelihood method, revealed no signs of dark matter interactions beyond the expected background. The research sets firm limits on the cross section for WIMP (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) -nucleon elastic scattering, with a minimum prohibition at a cross section of 7.6 x 10^-46 cm2 when the WIMP mass is approximately 33 GeV/c^2.

The LUX data appears to conflict with low-mass WIMP signal interpretations from multiple recent direct detection experiments, signaling a new direction in the understanding and search for dark matter particles.

title: Lectures on holographic methods for condensed matter physics
abstract:
These notes are loosely based on lectures given at the CERN Winter School on
Supergravity, Strings and Gauge theories, February 2009 and at the IPM String
School in Tehran, April 2009. I have focused on a few concrete topics and also
on addressing questions that have arisen repeatedly. Background condensed
matter physics material is included as motivation and easy reference for the
high energy physics community. The discussion of holographic techniques
progresses from equilibrium, to transport and to superconductivity.
summary:
**Title:** Holographic Methods for Condensed Matter Physics: Bridging Two Realms

**Article:**
In a recent paper published in Classical and Quantum Gravity, physicist Sean A. Hartnoll delves into the application of holography – a concept often associated with high energy physics – to the field of condensed matter physics. The work, presented as a series of lectures at CERN and IPM string schools in 2009, aims to connect these two distinct areas by demonstrating the potential of supergravity methods for explaining complex phenomena in condensed matter systems. The paper progresses from discussing equilibrium properties to transport dynamics and superconductivity. The work builds upon past research in both physics domains, providing a useful reference for researchers hoping to advance understanding at the intersection of high energy and condensed matter physics.

title: hijing: A Monte Carlo model for multiple jet production in<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>pp</mml:mi></mml:math>,<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>pA</mml:mi></mml:math>, and<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>AA</mml:mi></mml:math>collisions
abstract: Combining perturbative-QCD inspired models for multiple jet production with low ${p}_{T}$ multistring phenomenology, we develop a Monte Carlo event generator hijing to study jet and multiparticle production in high energy $\mathrm{pp}$, $\mathrm{pA}$, and $\mathrm{AA}$ collisions. The model includes multiple minijet production, nuclear shadowing of parton distribution functions, and a schematic mechanism of jet interactions in dense matter. Glauber geometry for multiple collisions is used to calculate $\mathrm{pA}$ and $\mathrm{AA}$ collisions. The phenomenological parameters are adjusted to reproduce essential features of $\mathrm{pp}$ multiparticle production data for a wide energy range ($\sqrt{s}=5\ensuremath{-}2000$ GeV). Illustrative tests of the model on $p+A$ and light-ion $B+A$ data at $\sqrt{s}=20$ GeV/nucleon and predictions for Au+Au at energies of the BNL Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider ($\sqrt{s}=200$ GeV/nucleon) are given.
summary:
New Monte Carlo model developed to study jet production in high-energy particle collisions

Physicists Xin-Nian Wang and Miklós Gyulassy have created a new event generator, hijing, to analyze jet and multiparticle production in proton-proton (pp), proton-nucleus (pA), and nucleus-nucleus (AA) collisions. The model combines perturbative quantum chromodynamics (QCD) inspired models for multiple jet production with low transverse momentum multistring phenomenology.

It includes multiple minijet production, nuclear shadowing of parton distribution functions, and a schematic mechanism of jet interactions in dense matter. The model incorporates Glauber geometry to calculate pA and AA collisions, and parameters are adjusted to match various energy ranges of pp multiparticle data (5-2000 GeV).

Initial tests demonstrate the application's potential on pA and light ion data at 20 GeV/nucleon, with predictions for Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV/nucleon offered. This work contributes to our understanding of particle physics in high-energy collisions, particularly those involving nucleons and dense matter formations.

title: Heterotic String
abstract: A new type of superstring theory is constructed as a chiral combination of the closed $D=26$ bosonic and $D=10$ fermionic strings. The theory is supersymmetric, Lorentz invariant, and free of tachyons. Consistency requires the gauge group to be $\frac{\mathrm{Spin}(32)}{{Z}_{2}}$ or ${E}_{8}\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}{E}_{8}$.
summary:
Paper Title: New Superstring Theory Unveiled, Free of Troublesome Tachyons

The latest work published in Physical Review Letters by David J. Gross, Jeffrey A. Harvey, Emil J. Martinec, and Ryan Rohm presents a groundbreaking superstring theory that combines elements from the 26-dimensional bosonic string and 10-dimensional fermionic strings.

This new theory, situated within the broader field of physics, aims to surpass previous theories by being free of tachyons - unstable particles that have been a persistent challenge in string theory research and superstring theory specifically. The consistency of this novel approach necessitates a gauge group of either $\frac{\mathrm{Spin}(32)}{{Z}_{2}}$ or ${E}_{8}\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{} {E}_{8}$, paving the way for further exploration into heterotic string theory.

title: A measurement of the spin asymmetry and determination of the structure function g1 in deep inelastic muon-proton scattering
abstract: The spin asymmetry in deep inelastic scattering of longitudinally polarised muons by longitudinally polarised protons has been measured over a large x range (0.01<x<0.7). The spin-dependent structure function g1(x) for the proton has been determined and its integral over x found to be 0.114±0.012±0.026, in disagreement with the Ellis-Jaffe sum rule. Assuming the validity of the Bjorken sum rule, this result implies a significant negative value for the integral of g1 for the neutron. These values for the integrals of g1 lead to the conclusion that the total quark spin constitutes a rather small fraction of the spin of the nucleon.
summary:
Headline:
New Study Reveals Surprising Spin Asymmetry Discovery in Proton-Muon Collisions

Summary:
A group of scientists have made a significant finding in the field of physics after measuring the spin asymmetry in the deep inelastic scattering of polarised muons with protons. The study, published in Physics Letters B, found that although the integral of g1 for the proton deviated from the Ellis-Jaffe sum rule, it implies a negative value for the neutron's integral if the Bjorken sum rule is valid. This suggests that the total quark spin contributes little to the spin of the nucleon, challenging our understanding of the inner workings of protons and neutrons.

title: An effective field theory for collinear and soft gluons: Heavy to light decays
abstract:
We construct the Lagrangian for an effective theory of highly energetic
quarks with energy Q, interacting with collinear and soft gluons. This theory
has two low energy scales, the transverse momentum of the collinear particles,
p_perp, and the scale p_perp^2/Q. The heavy to light currents are matched onto
operators in the effective theory at one-loop and the renormalization group
equations for the corresponding Wilson coefficients are solved. This running is
used to sum Sudakov logarithms in inclusive B -> X_s gamma and B -> X_u \ell nu
decays. We also show that the interactions with collinear gluons preserve the
relations for the soft part of the form factor for heavy to light decays found
by Charles et al., establishing these relations in the large energy limit of
QCD.
summary:
Title: Physicists Advance Understanding of High-Energy Quark Decays

Subheading: New Effective Field Theory Simplifies Collinear and Soft Gluon Interactions

Physics journal, Physical review. D, has published a groundbreaking study titled "An effective field theory for collinear and soft gluons: Heavy to light decays," led by C. Bauer, Sean Fleming, Dan Pirjol, and Iain W. Stewart. In this research, the team constructs a Lagrangian for an effective theory of highly energetic quarks, interacting with collinear and soft gluons, which are key particles in quantum chromodynamics (QCD).

The authors introduce two low energy scales to their effective theory: the transverse momentum of the collinear particles (p_perp) and the scale p_perp^2/Q. This innovative approach enables one-loop matching onto operators in the effective theory, providing crucial insights into heavy to light currents and solving renormalization group equations for corresponding Wilson coefficients.

The research team has successfully applied their findings to sum Sudakov logarithms in inclusive B –> X_s gamma and B –> X_u ℓν decays, offering a significant advancement in understanding such processes in the realm of high-energy physics. Moreover, they verify and extend the relations for the soft part of the form factor for heavy to light decays, as found by Charles et al., establishing these important findings in QCD's large energy limit. This work represents an essential step toward simplifying complex interactions within particle physics and will likely stimulate further research on high-energy quark decays.

title: Results from a Search for Dark Matter in the Complete LUX Exposure
abstract: We report constraints on spin-independent weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP)-nucleon scattering using a 3.35×10^{4} kg day exposure of the Large Underground Xenon (LUX) experiment. A dual-phase xenon time projection chamber with 250 kg of active mass is operated at the Sanford Underground Research Facility under Lead, South Dakota (USA). With roughly fourfold improvement in sensitivity for high WIMP masses relative to our previous results, this search yields no evidence of WIMP nuclear recoils. At a WIMP mass of 50 GeV c^{-2}, WIMP-nucleon spin-independent cross sections above 2.2×10^{-46} cm^{2} are excluded at the 90% confidence level. When combined with the previously reported LUX exposure, this exclusion strengthens to 1.1×10^{-46} cm^{2} at 50 GeV c^{-2}.
summary:
Title: Major Steps Forward in Dark Matter Search as LUX Experiment Unveils New Results

Summary:
A diverse team of physicists, led by D. S. Akerib and others, have published their findings from the Large Underground Xenon (LUX) experiment in the prestigious journal Physical Review Letters. The study, which took place deep beneath Lead in South Dakota's Sanford Underground Research Facility, aimed to discover weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), one of the leading dark matter candidates. Using a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber with 250 kg of active mass, the researchers have made significant strides in detection technology and sensitivity compared to previous results. Despite confirming no evidence of WIMP nuclear recoils during their 3.35×10^{4} kg day exposure, the team was able to exclude WIMP-nucleon spin-independent cross sections above 2.2×10^{-46} cm^{2} at a WIMP mass of 50 GeV c^{-2}, marking an important step in the search for dark matter. When combined with previous LUX data, this exclusion strengthens to 1.1×10^{-46} cm^{2} at 50 GeV c^{-2}. The study furthers our understanding of the mystery surrounding dark matter and sets a stronger baseline for future experiments in the field.

title: Commutator of the Quark Mass Matrices in the Standard Electroweak Model and a Measure of Maximal<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>CP</mml:mi></mml:math>Nonconservation
abstract: The structure of the quark mass matrices in the standard electroweak model is investigated. The commutator of the quark mass matrices is found to provide a convention-independent measure of $\mathrm{CP}$ nonconservation. The question of maximal $\mathrm{CP}$ nonconservation is discussed. The present experimental data indicate that nowhere is $\mathrm{CP}$ nonconservation maximal.
summary:
**Physicist Proposes New Measure for Symmetry Violation in Standard Model**

In a groundbreaking paper published in Physical Review Letters, physicist Cecilia Jarlskog explores the structure of quark mass matrices within the standard electroweak model.

Jarlskog proposes that the commutator of quark mass matrices offers a convention-independent measure for CP nonconservation, a phenomenon linked to the violation of fundamental symmetries in particle physics. Jarlskog's work builds upon earlier research into CP (charge conjugation and parity) nonconservation, yet provides new implications about the extent to which this symmetry is violated.

With the current experimental data suggesting that maximal CP nonconservation remains undetected, this study offers a fresh perspective to ongoing investigations in particle physics.

title: Evidence for High-Energy Extraterrestrial Neutrinos at the IceCube Detector
abstract: Extraterrestrial Neutrinos Neutrinos are thought to be produced in astrophysical sources outside our solar system but, up until recently, they had only been observed from one supernova in 1987. Aartsen et al. ( 10.1126/science.1242856 ; see the cover) report data obtained between 2010 and 2012 with the IceCube neutrino detector that reveal the presence of a high-energy neutrino flux containing the most energetic neutrinos ever observed, including 28 events at energies between 30 and 1200 TeV. Although the origin of this flux is unknown, the findings are consistent with expectations for a neutrino population with origins outside the solar system.
summary:
**Headline:**
"IceCube Neutrino Detector Sparks Extraterrestrial Life Debate with Discovery of High-Energy Neutrinos"

**Summary:**
In a groundbreaking discovery, scientists from the IceCube Collaboration – led by M. G. Aartsen – have detected high-energy neutrinos at the South Pole's IceCube Detector. This finding marks the first observation of such particles coming from sources beyond our solar system, surpassing the previous record set by a 1987 supernova. With an unprecedented energy range between 30 and 1200 TeV encompassed in 28 events, this extraterrestrial neutrino flux could stem from astrophysical phenomena outside our solar system, potentially opening the door to new speculations about distant cosmic mysteries and potential signs of extraterrestrial life. title: Hierarchy of Interactions in Unified Gauge Theories
abstract: We present a general formalism for calculating the renormalization effects which make strong interactions strong in simple gauge theories of strong, electromagnetic, and weak interactions. In an SU(5) model the superheavy gauge bosons arising in the spontaneous breakdown to observed interactions have mass perhaps as large as ${10}^{17}$ GeV, almost the Planck mass. Mixing-angle predictions are substantially modified.
summary:
Title: New Formalism Proposes Strong Interactions Strengthening in Gauge Theories

Subhead: Physicists Offer a Roadmap for Understanding Subatomic Forces

In an exciting development, researchers Howard Georgi, Helen R. Quinn, and Steven Weinberg have presented a novel formalism to calculate the effects responsible for making strong interactions stronger, as observed in simple gauge theories of strong, electromagnetic, and weak interactions. The new method may hold the key to understanding the complex workings of subatomic particles, according to their paper published in Physical Review Letters.

In the proposed framework, the masses of superheavy gauge bosons, arising from the spontaneous breakdown of observed interactions, reach values as high as ${10}^{17}$ GeV, approaching the Planck mass. This means that these particles could potentially hold crucial insights about the fundamental structure of the universe itself. Furthermore, the theory's predictions for mixing angles are substantially modified, providing fresh perspectives on the nature of subatomic interactions within a unified gauge framework.

title: Locally Supersymmetric Grand Unification
abstract: A locally supersymmetric grand unification program is proposed which couples the $N=1$ supergravity multiplet to an arbitrary grand unified gauge group with any number of left-handed chiral multiplets and a gauge vector multiplet. A specific model is discussed where it is shown that not only do the gravitational interactions eliminate the degeneracy of the vacuum state encountered in global supersymmetry, but simultaneously they can break both supersymmetry and SU(2) \ensuremath{\bigotimes} U(1) down to a residual $\mathrm{SU}{(3)}^{c}\ensuremath{\bigotimes}\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry at \ensuremath{\sim}300 GeV.
summary:
New Physics Proposal Reveals Insights into Grand Unification

Physicists Ali H. Chamseddine, R. Arnowitt, and Pran Nath propose a groundbreaking theory in the Physical Review Letters journal. Known as Locally Supersymmetric Grand Unification, the program unites physics' grandest ideas – particle physics and supersymmetry - with an ambitious goal to create a single framework for all known fundamental interactions.

The team introduces a model where the gravitational interactions of $N=1$ supergravity multiplets can simultaneously break both supersymmetry and the SU(2) \ensuremath{\bigotimes} U(1) down to a residual $\mathrm{SU}{(3)}^{c}\ensuremath{\bigotimes}\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry at approximately 300 GeV. This breakthrough offers a potential solution for resolving the vacuum state degeneracy problem experienced in previous global supersymmetry models.

title: Accurate charge-dependent nucleon-nucleon potential at fourth order of chiral perturbation theory
abstract: We present the first nucleon-nucleon potential at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (fourth order) of chiral perturbation theory. Charge-dependence is included up to next-to-leading order of the isospin-violation scheme. The accuracy for the reproduction of the NN data below 290 MeV lab. energy is comparable to the one of phenomenological high-precision potentials. Since NN potentials of order three and less are known to be deficient in quantitative terms, the present work shows that the fourth order is necessary and sufficient for a reliable NN potential derived from chiral effective Lagrangians. The new potential provides a promising starting point for exact few-body calculations and microscopic nuclear structure theory (including chiral many-body forces derived on the same footing).
summary:
Title: New, Accurate Charged Nucleon Potential Developed in Fourth Order of Chiral Perturbation Theory

Subhead: Physics breakthrough could advance nuclear science research

In an important contribution to nuclear physics, researchers D. R. Entem and R. Machleidt have developed a new nucleon-nucleon potential at fourth order (next-to-next-to-next-to-leading) of chiral perturbation theory. This is the first such potential presented which includes charge-dependence up to next-to-leading order in the isospin-violation scheme.

The new potential achieved comparable accuracy for the reproduction of nuclear data below 290 MeV lab energy to that of existing high-precision phenomenological potentials, marking a significant improvement over previous potentials of order three or less that have been found to fall short in quantitative terms. This work indicates that the fourth order derivation from chiral effective Lagrangians is both necessary and sufficient for a reliable NN potential.

The novel potential paves the way for more exact few-body calculations and microscopic nuclear structure theory, offering promising new insights into the behavior of nucleons in atomic nuclei. The work has been published in Physical Review C.

title: All-Optical Magnetic Recording with Circularly Polarized Light
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate that the magnetization can be reversed in a reproducible manner by a single 40 femtosecond circularly polarized laser pulse, without any applied magnetic field. This optically induced ultrafast magnetization reversal previously believed impossible is the combined result of femtosecond laser heating of the magnetic system to just below the Curie point and circularly polarized light simultaneously acting as a magnetic field. The direction of this opto-magnetic switching is determined only by the helicity of light. This finding reveals an ultrafast and efficient pathway for writing magnetic bits at record-breaking speeds.

This light-induced "opto-magnetic" switching offers an ultrafast and efficient method for writing magnetic bits at record-breaking speeds.

This research article, published in Physical Review Letters, builds upon studies about femtosecond lasers, ultrashort pulses, circular polarization, and magnetization, offering a potential solution to developing faster and more efficient data storage technologies.

title: String Theory
abstract: String Theory, first published in 1998, comprises two volumes which provide a comprehensive and pedagogic account of the subject. Volume 2 begins with an introduction to supersymmetric string theories and presents the important advances of recent years. The first three chapters introduce the type I, type II, and heterototic superstring theories and their interactions. The next two chapters present important recent discoveries about strongly coupled strings, beginning with a detailed treatment of D-branes and their dynamics, and covering string duality, M-theory, and black hole entropy. The final chapters are concerned with four-dimensional string theories, showing how some of the simplest string models connect with previous ideas for unifying the Standard Model. They collect many important results on world-sheet and spacetime symmetries. An appendix summarizes the necessary background on fermions and supersymmetry. An essential text and reference for graduate students and researchers interested in superstring theory.

title: New parton distribution functions from a global analysis of quantum chromodynamics
abstract: Here, we present new parton distribution functions (PDFs) up to next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) from the CTEQ-TEA global analysis of quantum chromodynamics. These differ from previous CT PDFs in several respects, including the use of data from LHC experiments and the new D0 charged lepton rapidity asymmetry data, as well as the use of more flexible parametrization of PDFs that, in particular, allows a better fit to different combinations of quark flavors. Predictions for important LHC processes, especially Higgs boson production at 13 TeV, are presented. These CT14 PDFs include a central set and error sets in the Hessian representation. For completeness, we also present the CT14 PDFs determined at the leading order (LO) and the next-to-leading order (NLO) in QCD. Besides these general-purpose PDF sets, we provide a series of (N)NLO sets with various α<sub>s</sub> values and additional sets in general-mass variable flavor number (GM-VFN) schemes, to deal with heavy partons, with up to 3, 4, and 6 active flavors.

title: Glauber Modeling in High-Energy Nuclear Collisions
abstract: We review the theoretical background, experimental techniques, and phenomenology of what is known in relativistic heavy ion physics as the Glauber model, which is used to calculate geometric quantities. A brief history of the original Glauber model is presented, with emphasis on its development into the purely classical, geometric picture used for present-day data analyses. Distinctions are made between the optical limit and Monte Carlo approaches, which are often used interchangeably but have some essential differences in particular contexts. The methods used by the four RHIC experiments are compared and contrasted, although the end results are reassuringly similar for the various geometric observables. Finally, several important RHIC measurements are highlighted that rely on geometric quantities, estimated from Glauber calculations, to draw insight from experimental observables. The status and future of Glauber modeling in the next generation of heavy ion physics studies is briefly discussed.

The analysis offers insights into the history, techniques, and practical applications of the model, which have evolved from its original form into a purely classical, geometric picture essential for contemporary data analyses. Distinctions are made between the optical limit and Monte Carlo approaches, with each method's unique benefits emphasized in specific contexts. The research highlights comparisons among four RHIC experiments, revealing reassuringly consistent results across different observables. Important nuclear collision measurements relying on geometric quantities, estimated from Glauber calculations, are underscored as offering key insights into experimental data. Looking ahead to future heavy ion physics studies, the paper discusses the current status and anticipated developments in Glauber modeling.

title: Gluon distribution functions for very large nuclei at small transverse momentum
abstract: We show that the gluon distribution function for very large nuclei may be computed for small transverse momentum as correlation functions of an ultraviolet finite two dimensional Euclidean field theory. abstract: We explore the consequences of the assumption that the direct and induced weak neutral currents in an $\mathrm{SU}(2)\ensuremath{\bigotimes}\mathrm{U}(1)$ gauge theory conserve all quark flavors naturally, i.e., for all values of the parameters of the theory. This requires that all quarks of a given charge and helicity must have the same values of weak ${T}_{3}$ and ${\stackrel{\ensuremath{\rightarrow}}{T}}^{2}$. If all quarks have charge +2/3 or -1/3 the only acceptable theories are the "standard" and "pure vector" models, or their generalizations to six or more quarks. In addition, there are severe constraints on the couplings of Higgs bosons, which apparently cannot be satisfied in pure vector models. We also consider the possibility that neutral currents conserve strangeness but not charm. A natural seven-quark model of this sort is described. The experimental consequences of charm nonconservation in direct or induced neutral currents are found to be quite dramatic.
summary:
Paper Title: Conserving Nature's Neutral Current Flavors: A New Approach to Particle Physics

In a groundbreaking work published in "Physical Review D", Nobel laureates Sheldon L. Glashow and Steven Weinberg propose a novel approach to understand the conservation laws governing weak neutral currents within an SU(2)⊗U(1) gauge theory.

Their research, focusing on quarks and their associated quantum numbers, aims to naturally conserve all quark flavors under these conservation laws, regardless of the parameters of the theory. They find that if all quarks carry charges +2/3 or -1/3, only the "standard" and "pure vector" models, or their six-quark extensions, are acceptable. However, they also conclude that pure vector models exhibit severe constraints on Higgs boson couplings which seem difficult to satisfy in these models alone.

More intriguingly, the study investigates the possibility of neutral currents conserving strangeness but not charm, revealing a potential seven-quark model and significant experimental implications for charm nonconservation in direct or induced neutral currents.

title: Observation of Top Quark Production in<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">p</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>¯</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">p</mml:mi></mml:math>Collisions with the Collider Detector at Fermilab
abstract: We establish the existence of the top quark using a 67pb[superscript −1] data sample of [¯ over p]p collisions at √s = 1.8TeV collected with the Collider Detector at Fermilab (CDF). Employing techniques similar to those we previously published, we observe a signal consistent with t[¯ over t] decay to WWb[¯ over b], but inconsistent with the background prediction by 4.8σ. Additional evidence for the top quark is provided by a peak in the reconstructed mass distribution. We measure the top quark mass to be 176±8(stat)±10(syst)GeV/c[superscript 2], and the t[¯ over t] production cross section to be 6.8[+3.6 over −2.4]pb.
summary:
Headline: Scientists Confirm Top Quark Existence in Historic Collider Study

Summary: A team of researchers, led by F. Abe et al., have announced the discovery of the top quark at the Collider Detector at Fermilab (CDF), using data from 67 pb-1 of proton–antiproton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 1.8 TeV. The study builds on previous research, employing similar techniques to identify the decay of top quarks into WWb-bar, and finds a signal that is 4.8 standard deviations away from the expected background. Additionally, the data reveals a peak in the reconstructed mass distribution, further supporting the existence of the top quark. The team reports a measured top quark mass of 176±8 (stat)±10 (syst) GeV/c² and a t-bar-t production cross section of 6.8+3.6 over -2.4 pb in this landmark finding within the realm of high-energy physics.

title: The role of resonances in chiral perturbation theory
abstract: The strong interactions of low-lying meson resonances (spin <= 1) with the octet of pseudoscalar mesons ( pi, K, eta) are considered to lowest order in the derivative expansion of chiral SU(3). The resonance contributions to the coupling constants of the O( p4) effective chiral lagrangian involving pseudoscalar fields only are determined. These low-energy coupling constants are found to be dominated by the resonance contributions. Although we do not treat the vector and axial-vector mesons as gauge bosons of local chiral symmetry, vector meson dominance emerges as a prominent result of our analysis. As a further application of chiral resonance couplings, we calculate the electromagnetic pion mass difference to lowest order in chiral perturbation theory with explicit resonance fields.

Their findings suggest that these resonance contributions significantly impact the coupling constants of the effective chiral lagrangian involving only pseudo-scalar fields. The study also finds that vector meson dominance emerges as a significant result, although the research does not treat vector and axial-vector mesons as local chiral symmetry's gauge bosons. As an extension of their work, the researchers also calculate the electromagnetic pion mass difference to the lowest order in chiral perturbation theory, incorporating explicit resonance fields. This study furthers our understanding of strong interaction physics and its underlying mechanics.

title: Applications of the Chiral<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mn/><mml:mo>⊗</mml:mo><mml:mi>U</mml:mi><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn><mml:mo>)</mml:mo><mml:mn/></mml:math>Algebra of Current Densities
abstract: Consequences of the local commutation relations of vector and axial currents proposed by Gell-Mann are explored: (1) A recipe for detecting and isolating Schwinger terms in the commutators, proportional to derivatives of the $\ensuremath{\delta}$ function, is discussed. (2) Under assumptions of smooth asymptotic behavior of form factors for forward scattering of the isovector current from a proton, we show that the $U(3)\ensuremath{\bigotimes}U(3)$ algebra for the time components of the currents implies the $U(6)\ensuremath{\bigotimes}U(6)$ algebra for space components, at least for spin-averaged diagonal single-particle states. (3) The derivation of the Adler-Weisberger formula for $\frac{{G}_{A}}{{G}_{V}}$ is sharpened by giving arguments that, at fixed energy, the forward $\ensuremath{\pi}\ensuremath{-}p$ Green's function satisfies an unsubtracted dispersion relation in the pion mass. (4) A lower bound for inelastic electron-nucleon scattering at high momentum transfer is derived on the basis of $U(6)\ensuremath{\bigotimes}U(6)$. (5) The contribution of very virtual photons to the hyperfine anomaly in hydrogen is shown to be related to an equal-time commutator of currents; this contribution is crudely estimated to be 4 parts per million (ppm). (6) The logarithmically divergent part of electromagnetic mass differences of hadrons is shown to be proportional to matrix elements of the equal-time commutator of the electromagnetic current with its time derivative. It is suggested that this "divergent" part be identified with the Coleman-Glashow "tadpoles"; this suggestion is discussed in the framework of a simple quark model. (7) The logarithmically divergent part of the electromagnetic correction to the process ${\ensuremath{\pi}}^{\ensuremath{-}}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}{\ensuremath{\pi}}^{0}+{e}^{\ensuremath{-}}+\overline{\ensuremath{\nu}}$ is, on the basis of the $U(6)\ensuremath{\bigotimes}U(6)$ current algebra, shown to be nonvanishing, and is computed. (8) A speculative argument is presented that the rate ${e}^{+}+{e}^{\ensuremath{-}}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}\mathrm{hadrons}$ is comparable to the rate ${e}^{+}+{e}^{\ensuremath{-}}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}{\ensuremath{\mu}}^{+}+{\ensuremath{\mu}}^{\ensuremath{-}}$ in the limit of large energies.

The study offers a fresh perspective on diverse aspects of nuclear and particle physics, contributing to ongoing efforts in the field.

title: Infrared singularities and massive fields
abstract: We examine some problems associated with the low-momentum behavior of gauge theories and other renormalizable field theories. Our main interest is in the infrared structure of unbroken non-Abelian gauge theories and how this is affected by the presence of other heavy fields coupled to the massless gauge fields. It is shown in the context of a simple model of gauge mesons coupled to massive fermions that the heavy fields decouple at low momenta except for their contribution to renormalization effects. This result is used to discuss the mass-shell structure of the fermion propagator. The decoupling theorem is then stated for a general renormalizable theory and applied to some interesting examples. One is a more general gauge theory which makes use of the Higgs mechanism and attempts to unify the elementary particle forces. Another is the connection of the linear and nonlinear $\ensuremath{\sigma}$ models in the limit ${m}_{\ensuremath{\sigma}}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}\ensuremath{\infty}$.

The scientists propose a simple model of gauge mesons coupled to massive fermions, revealing that heavy fields decouple at low momenta except for their contribution to renormalization effects. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the mass-shell structure of the fermion propagator and have implications for more complex theories such as a unified gauge theory approach to elementary particle forces and the connection between linear and nonlinear sigma models in the limit of infinite mass.

title: Scaling Laws at Large Transverse Momentum
abstract: The application of simple dimensional counting to bound states of pointlike particles enables us to derive scaling laws for the asymptotic energy dependence of electromagnetic and hadronic scattering at fixed c.m. angle which only depend on the number of constituent fields of the hadrons. Assuming quark constituents, some of the s→∞, fixed-ts predictions are ($\\frac{dσ}{dt}$)<sub>πp→πp</sub>~s<sup>-8</sup>, ($\\frac{dσ}{dt}$)<sub>pp→pp</sub>~s<sup>-10</sup>, ($\\frac{dσ}{dt}$)<sub>γp→πp</sub>~s<sup>-7</sup>, ($\\frac{dσ}{dt}$)<sub>γp→γp</sub>~s<sup>-6</sup>, F<sub>π</sub>(q<sup>2</sup>)~(q<sup>2</sup>)<sup>-1</sup>, and F<sub>1p</sub>(q<sup>2</sup>)~(q<sup>2</sup>)<sup>-2</sup>. We show that such scaling laws are characteristic of renormalizable field theories satisfying certain conditions.
summary:
In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review Letters, physicists Stanley J. Brodsky and Glennys R. Farrar have derived new scaling laws for energy dependence at large transverse momentum in particle scattering. The researchers apply a method involving dimensional counting to bound states of pointlike particles to make their predictions, focusing specifically on hadrons made up of quark constituents.

The study suggests that the cross-section for interactions between particles, like pions and protons, decreases dramatically with energy (squared) as follows: for πp→πp it's ~s⁻⁸, for pp→pp it's ~s⁻¹⁰, and for γp→πp it's ~s⁻7. Similarly, the study finds that the scattering between a photon (γ) and a proton (p) would exhibit a ~s⁻6 scaling. The authors also illustrate how these scaling laws are characteristic of renormalizable field theories meeting specific conditions.

abstract: The spectra and dominant decay couplings of ${Q}^{2}{\overline{Q}}^{2}$ mesons are presented as calculated in the quark-bag model. Certain known ${0}^{+}$ mesons [$\ensuremath{\epsilon}(700),{S}^{*},\ensuremath{\delta},\ensuremath{\kappa}$] are assigned to the lightest cryptoexotic ${Q}^{2}{\overline{Q}}^{2}$ nonet. The usual quark-model ${0}^{+}$ nonet ($Q\overline{Q} L=1$) must lie higher in mass. All other ${Q}^{2}{\overline{Q}}^{2}$ mesons are predicted to be broad, heavy, and usually inelastic in formation processes. Other ${Q}^{2}{\overline{Q}}^{2}$ states which may be experimentally prominent are discussed.

Subhead: Jaffe's Phenomenon of $Q^2\bar{Q}^2$ Mesons Offer Fresh Perspectives in Particle Physics

A new article published in Physical Review D. Particles, Fields, Gravitation and Cosmology proposes fresh insights into the world of particle physics. Noted physicist R.J. Jaffe presents the spectra and dominant decay couplings of $Q^2\bar{Q}^2$ mesons, using the quark-bag model as his framework.

This research aims to revise our understanding of certain known $0^+$ mesons like epsilon(700), S*, delta, and kappa by classifying them as the lightest cryptoexotic $Q^2\bar{Q}^2$ nonet. Traditional quark-model $0^+$ nonets (Q\ Mal1) are hypothesized to have a higher mass. Jaffe's model predicts that other $Q^2\bar{Q}^2$ mesons will be broad, heavy, and typically inelastic during formation processes. The article also discusses additional $Q^2\bar{Q}^2$ states that could become experimentally prominent in the future.

With this work, Jaffe continues to push the boundaries of particle physics and meson theory, offering a new perspective on hadron compositions as well as potential paths for further investigation in the field.

title: Soft-collinear factorization in effective field theory
abstract: The factorization of soft and ultrasoft gluons from collinear particles is shown at the level of operators in an effective field theory. Exclusive hadronic factorization and inclusive partonic factorization follow as special cases. The leading order Lagrangian is derived using power counting and gauge invariance in the effective theory. Several species of gluons are required, and softer gluons appear as background fields to gluons with harder momenta. Two examples are given: the factorization of soft gluons in B->D pi, and the soft-collinear convolution for the B->Xs gamma spectrum.
summary:
In the realm of physics, a groundbreaking study offered by researchers C. Bauer, Dan Pirjol, and Iain W. Stewart has made significant strides in understanding particle interactions through the development of an effective field theory. The study focuses on 'soft-collinear factorization', which is a key concept in particle physics.

The paper demonstrates that soft and ultrasoft gluons can be disassociated from collinear particles at the level of operators within this effective field theory. This theory, applied to both exclusive hadronic factorization and inclusive partonic factorization, provides insights into the behavior of gluons - fundamental particles in the strong nuclear force - under complex interactions.

The study's results reveal that softer gluons function as background fields for harder ones, offering important implications for various scenarios including the decay of a B-meson into a D-meson and a pi, and the B->Xs gamma spectrum. This work serves to advance our understanding of these intricate processes within particle physics, paving the way for further exploration and discovery in this field.

title: Averages of b-hadron, c-hadron, and $$\tau $$ τ -lepton properties as of summer 2016
abstract: This article reports world averages of measurements of b-hadron, c-hadron, and $\\tau $ -lepton properties obtained by the Heavy Flavor Averaging Group using results available through summer 2016. For the averaging, common input parameters used in the various analyses are adjusted (rescaled) to common values, and known correlations are taken into account. The averages include branching fractions, lifetimes, neutral meson mixing parameters, $C\\!P$ violation parameters, parameters of semileptonic decays, and Cabbibo–Kobayashi–Maskawa matrix elements.
summary:
**Physicists unveil latest findings on subatomic particles**

A multinational team of researchers has published new data on the properties of b-hadrons, c-hadrons, and tau leptons, shedding light on the behaviour of these fundamental particles. The study, led by Y. Amhis and colleagues, appears in 'The European Physical Journal C'.

Drawing from various analyses up until summer 2016, the team adjusted common input parameters to create harmonized averages for branching fractions, lifetimes, mixing parameters, CP violation parameters, semileptonic decay parameters, and Cabbibo–Kobayashi–Maskawa matrix elements. This work builds upon previous research in particle physics and nuclear physics, advancing our understanding of the intricate world of hadrons and leptons to further probe the mysteries of the universe.

title: Color superconductivity in dense quark matter
abstract: Matter at high density and low temperature is expected to be a color superconductor, which is a degenerate Fermi gas of quarks with a condensate of Cooper pairs near the Fermi surface that induces color Meissner effects. At the highest densities, where the QCD coupling is weak, rigorous calculations are possible, and the ground state is a particularly symmetric state, the color-flavor locked (CFL) phase. The CFL phase is a superfluid, an electromagnetic insulator, and breaks chiral symmetry. The effective theory of the low-energy excitations in the CFL phase is known and can be used, even at more moderate densities, to describe its physical properties. At lower densities the CFL phase may be disfavored by stresses that seek to separate the Fermi surfaces of the different flavors, and comparison with the competing alternative phases, which may break translation and/or rotation invariance, is done using phenomenological models. We review the calculations that underlie these results, and then discuss transport properties of several color-superconducting phases and their consequences for signatures of color superconductivity in neutron stars.
summary:
Headline: New Study Sheds Light on Color Superconductivity in Star Matter

Summary:
A new study published in Reviews of Modern Physics delves into the intriguing concept of color superconductivity, a state that could be found in matter at high density and low temperature, like that found in neutron stars. The researchers, including Mark Alford, Andreas Schmitt, Krishna Rajagopal, and Thomas Schäfer, focus on the degenerate Fermi gas of quarks known as the color-flavor locked (CFL) phase. This phase, which occurs at the highest densities where the QCD coupling is weak, is a superfluid, an electromagnetic insulator, and breaks chiral symmetry. The study establishes an effective theory for the low-energy excitations in the CFL phase, which can be used to describe its physical properties even at more moderate densities. However, at lower densities, the CFL phase may be overshadowed by competing phases that break translation and rotation invariance. The team discusses the transport properties of various color-superconducting phases and their potential implications for signs of color superconductivity in neutron stars.

title: Asymptotically Free Gauge Theories. I
abstract: Asymptotically free gauge theories of the strong interactions are constructed and analyzed. The reasons for doing this are recounted, including a review of renormalization-group techniques and their application to scaling phenomena. The renormalization-group equations are derived for Yang-Mills theories. The parameters that enter into the equations are calculated to lowest order and it is shown that these theories are asymptotically free. More specifically the effective coupling constant, which determines the ultraviolet behavior of the theory, vanishes for large spacelike momenta. Fermions are incorporated and the construction of realistic models is discussed. We propose that the strong interactions be mediated by a "color" gauge group which commutes with SU(3) \ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{} SU(3). The problem of symmetry breaking is discussed. It appears likely that this would have a dynamical origin. It is suggested that the gauge symmetry might not be broken and that the severe infrared singularities prevent the occurrence of noncolor singlet physical states. The deep-inelastic structure functions, as well as the electron-positron total annihilation cross section are analyzed. Scaling obtains up to calculable logarithmic corrections, and the naive light-cone or parton-model results follow. The problems of incorporating scalar mesons and breaking the symmetry by the Higgs mechanism are explained in detail.
summary:
"New Gauge Theory Approach Unveiled for Strong Interactions"

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review, physicists David J. Gross and Frank Wilczek present a novel approach to understanding strong interactions - the forces that bind atomic nuclei together. The paper, titled "Asymptotically Free Gauge Theories," delves into the construction and analysis of gauge theories that could potentially explain the behavior of these powerful forces.

The research is rooted in renormalization-group techniques, used to interpret scaling phenomena, and applied to Yang-Mills theories. The researchers demonstrate that these theories exhibit an intriguing property known as asymptotic freedom, where effective coupling constants vanish for large spacelike momenta. Fermions are also integrated into the models, bringing us a step closer to realistic applications.

The authors propose a "color" gauge group, which could potentially mediate strong interactions, and discuss the problem of symmetry breaking, suggesting it may have a dynamic origin. The study also touches upon deep-inelastic structure functions and electron-positron total annihilation cross sections, showing that scaling holds up to logarithmic corrections, supporting the parton model results. However, challenges such as incorporating scalar mesons and breaking symmetry by the Higgs mechanism still remain.

title: Dark Matter Results from 225 Live Days of XENON100 Data
abstract: We report on a search for particle dark matter with the XENON100 experiment, operated at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso for 13 months during 2011 and 2012. XENON100 features an ultralow electromagnetic background of (5.3 ± 0.6) × 10(-3) events/(keV(ee) × kg × day) in the energy region of interest. A blind analysis of 224.6 live days × 34 kg exposure has yielded no evidence for dark matter interactions. The two candidate events observed in the predefined nuclear recoil energy range of 6.6-30.5 keV(nr) are consistent with the background expectation of (1.0 ± 0.2) events. A profile likelihood analysis using a 6.6-43.3 keV(nr) energy range sets the most stringent limit on the spin-independent elastic weakly interacting massive particle-nucleon scattering cross section for weakly interacting massive particle masses above 8 GeV/c(2), with a minimum of 2 × 10(-45) cm(2) at 55 GeV/c(2) and 90% confidence level.
summary:
XENON100 Experiment Reveals No Evidence of Dark Matter Interaction
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A new study published in *Physical Review Letters* presents the findings of the experimental search for dark matter using the XENON100 detector, run for 13 months between 2011 and 2012. The experiment, housed at Italy's Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso, reported an incredibly low electromagnetic background rate, offering a unique opportunity to hunt for elusive dark matter particles.

An in-depth analysis of 224.6 live days and 34 kilograms of exposure revealed no evidence of dark matter interactions, with just two candidate events detected within the specified nuclear recoil energy range (6.6-30.5 keV(nr)). The study's authors used a sophisticated statistical analysis to set limits on spin-independent elastic weakly interacting massive particle-nucleon scattering cross section. Particularly, the limits are most stringent for weakly interacting massive particle masses above 8 GeV/c^2, with a minimum cross section of 2 × 10^-45 cm^2 at 55 GeV/c^2 and a 90% confidence level.

title: Left-right gauge symmetry and an "isoconjugate" model of<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>CP</mml:mi></mml:math>violation
abstract: Left-right symmetry in the starting gauge interactions provides the basis for an "isoconjugate" model of $\mathrm{CP}$ violation with the consequence that ${\ensuremath{\eta}}_{+\ensuremath{-}}={\ensuremath{\eta}}_{00}$. The magnitude of $\mathrm{CP}$ violation is naturally suppressed at least to the extent that $V+A$ interactions are suppressed in nature compared to the $V\ensuremath{-}A$ interactions. This allows the possibility that intrinsic $\mathrm{CP}$-violating phase (arising through spontaneous symmetry breaking, for example) may have a maximal character, which may reveal itself at intermediate high energies to possibly disappear at still higher energies. $\mathrm{CP}$ violation in leptonic, semileptonic, and $\ensuremath{\Delta}Y=0$ parity-violating nonleptonic interactions (which could contribute to the electric dipole moment of the neutron) arise on the one hand in fourth order of the weak gauge interactions and on the other via Yukawa interactions between fermions and leftover Higgs mesons as well as via ${W}_{L}\ensuremath{-}{W}_{R}$ mixing. The magnitude of the latter contributions may be limited to be less than or of order ${G}_{F}\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}{10}^{\ensuremath{-}4}$ in order that the experimentally observed relation ${\ensuremath{\eta}}_{+\ensuremath{-}}={\ensuremath{\eta}}_{00}$ may hold at least to a few percent. Thus the electric dipole moment of the neutron ${d}_{n}$ is expected to be less than or of order ${10}^{\ensuremath{-}24}e$ cm. $\mathrm{CP}$ violation in all $|\ensuremath{\Delta}S|=1$ nonleptonic decays ($Y\ensuremath{\rightarrow}N+\ensuremath{\pi}$, etc.) should, in general, have the same order of magnitude as $|{\ensuremath{\eta}}_{+\ensuremath{-}}|$.
summary:
Headline: Physicists propose new model for CP violation in particle interactions

Summary:
In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review D, physicists Rabindra N. Mohapatra and Jogesh C. Pati present an innovative "isoconjugate" model of CP (charge-parity) violation based on left-right symmetry. This new model could potentially explain the suppression of CP violation seen in nature, where V+A (vector plus axial vector) interactions are weaker compared to V-A interactions. The researchers suggest that at intermediate high energies, intrinsic CP-violating phases may exhibit maximal character, possibly vanishing at higher energies. The model further predicts CP violation in leptonic, semileptonic, and certain nonleptonic interactions, which might contribute to the electric dipole moment of the neutron, theoretically estimated to be less than or equal to ${10}^{-24} e$ cm. The study could have significant implications for understanding and predicting CP violation in various particle decays.

title: Strange matter
abstract: We explore the properties of quark matter in equilibrium with the weak interactions, containing comparable numbers of up, down, and strange quarks. Witten has recently conjectured that this "strange matter" may be absolutely stable. Using a Fermi-gas model including $O({\ensuremath{\alpha}}_{c})$ corrections we establish the conditions under which strange matter in bulk is stable and describe its characteristics. Augmenting our model with surface-tension and Coulomb effects we study strange matter with intermediate baryon number ${10}^{2}\ensuremath{\lesssim}A\ensuremath{\lesssim}{10}^{7}$. For low baryon numbers $A\ensuremath{\lesssim}{10}^{2}$, we replace the Fermi gas by the bag model and study shell effects and the approach to the bulk limit. Finally, we discuss the phenomenology of strange matter in all its forms.
summary:
**New Paper Suggests Absolute Stability of "Strange Matter"**

Physicists Edward Farhi and R.L. Jaffe, in a new study published in Physical Review D, explore the properties of a unique form of matter known as "strange matter." This matter contains equal numbers of up, down, and strange quarks, and according to a recent conjecture by Witten, it may be absolutely stable.

In their research, Farhi and Jaffe use a Fermi-gas model including $O({\ensuremath{\alpha}}_{c})$ corrections to establish the conditions under which this strange matter remains stable, detailing its characteristic properties. They also incorporate surface-tension and Coulomb effects to study intermediate-baryon number strange matter, that is, ranging from ${10}^{2}$ to ${10}^{7}$.

For low baryon numbers ($A\ensuremath{\lesssim}{10}^{2}$), the researchers replace the Fermi gas with the bag model and scrutinize shell effects as well as the transition towards the bulk limit. Finally, they discuss the various phenomenological aspects of strange matter in all its forms, shedding light on potential implications for particle physics and nuclear astrophysics.

title: Construction of high-qualityNNpotential models
abstract:
We present an updated version (Nijm93) of the Nijmegen soft-core potential,
which gives a much better description of the np data than the older version
(Nijm78). The chi^2 per datum is 1.87. The configuration-space and
momentum-space versions of this potential are exactly equivalent; a unique
feature among meson-theoretical potentials. We also present three new NN
potential models: a non-local Reid-like Nijmegen potential (NijmI), a local
version (NijmII), and an updated regularized version (Reid93) of the Reid
soft-core potential. These three potentials all have a nearly optimal chi^2 per
datum and can therefore be considered as alternative partial-wave analyses. All
potentials contain the proper charge-dependent one-pion-exchange tail. Fortran
code for the potentials can be obtained via anonymous ftp from
thef-nym.sci.kun.nl
summary:
Title: New Nijmegen Soft-Core Potential Models Improve Accuracy in Nuclear Physics

In a groundbreaking development, researchers led by V. G. J. Stoks have constructed high-quality Neutron-Neutron (NN) potential models reported in Physical Review C. The new models, an updated version of the Nijmegen soft-core potential with a significantly improved description of nuclear data, are named Nijm93. The unique selling point of these potentials is their exact equivalence between configuration space and momentum space, a feature not commonly found among meson-theoretical potentials.

Three additional NN potential models have been introduced alongside Nijm93: a non-local Reid-like Nijmegen potential (NijmI), a local version (NijmII), and an updated regularized version of the Reid soft-core potential (Reid93). These new models offer nearly optimal chi^2 per datum, making them viable alternatives for partial-wave analyses. All potentials incorporate the proper charge-dependent one-pion-exchange tail, further improving their accuracy and applicability in nuclear physics.

title: Sterile neutrinos as dark matter
abstract: The simplest model that can accomodate a viable nonbaryonic dark matter candidate is the standard electroweak theory with the addition of right-handed or sterile neutrinos. We reexamine this model and find that the sterile neutrinos can be either hot, warm, or cold dark matter. Since their only direct coupling is to left-handed or active neutrinos, the most efficient production mechanism is via neutrino oscillations. If the production rate is always less than the expansion rate, then these neutrinos will never be in thermal equilibrium. However, enough of them may be produced so that they provide the missing mass necessary for closure. We consider a single generation of neutrino fields $\left (\nu_L,\,\nu_R\right )$ with a Dirac mass, $\mu$, and a Majorana mass for the right-handed components only, $M$. For $M\gg \mu$ we show that the number density of sterile neutrinos is proportional to $\mu^2/M$ so that the energy density today is {\it independent of} $M$. However $M$ is crucial in determining the large scale structure of the Universe. In particular, $M\simeq 0.1-1.0 {\rm ~keV}$ leads to warm dark matter and a structure formation scenario that may have some advantages over both the standard hot and cold dark matter scenarios.
summary:
Title: "Sterile Neutrinos As Potential Dark Matter Candidates Explored in New Study"

New research published in Physical Review Letters by Scott Dodelson and Lawrence M. Widrow is shedding light on a potential solution for the mystery of dark matter, using the concept of sterile neutrinos as a candidate. The scientists are delving into a model that combines the Standard Electroweak Theory with right-handed or sterile neutrinos. By examining efficient production mechanisms via neutrino oscillations, they find these neutrinos could be any temperature of dark matter – hot, warm, or cold. The study reveals intriguing possibilities about structure formation, particularly suggesting that a Majorana mass for the right-handed components within the range of 0.1 to 1.0 keV could result in "warm" dark matter, offering advantages for understanding cosmic large scale structure over current hot and cold dark matter frameworks.

title: Dark Matter Candidates from Particle Physics and Methods of Detection
abstract: The identity of dark matter is a question of central importance in both astrophysics and particle physics. In the past, the leading particle candidates were cold and collisionless, and typically predicted missing energy signals at particle colliders. However, recent progress has greatly expanded the list of well-motivated candidates and the possible signatures of dark matter. This review begins with a brief summary of the standard model of particle physics and its outstanding problems. I then discuss several dark matter candidates motivated by these problems, including weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), superWIMPs, light gravitinos, hidden dark matter, sterile neutrinos, and axions. For each of these, I critically examine the particle physics motivations and present their expected production mechanisms, basic properties, and implications for direct and indirect detection, particle colliders, and astrophysical observations. Upcoming experiments will discover or exclude many of these candidates, and progress may open up an era of unprecedented synergy between studies of the largest and smallest observable length scales.
